titre: The Water-Diamond Paradox, Solved Three Times
accroche: Between 1871 and 1874, three economists unaware of one another publish, in three different countries, the same solution to a century-old riddle.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1776, in *The Wealth of Nations*, Adam Smith poses a riddle he does not solve: water, indispensable to life, is worth almost nothing to buy, while the diamond, which we can do without entirely, trades for a fortune. If a good's value measures its usefulness, water should be worth infinitely more than diamonds. For nearly a century, no economist finds a satisfactory way out: the labor theory of value, which explains price by the amount of labor needed to produce a good, stumbles over the same problem without solving it.

## Three Countries, One Answer, No Contact

The solution arrives almost at the same time, from three men who know nothing of one another. In 1871, in Manchester, William Stanley Jevons publishes *The Theory of Political Economy*; the same year, in Vienna, Carl Menger brings out his *Grundsätze der Volkswirthschaftslehre* (Principles of Economics); three years later, in Lausanne, Léon Walras publishes the first part of his *Éléments d'économie politique pure* (Elements of Pure Economics), without knowing the two earlier books. All three arrive at the same shift: it is not the total usefulness of a category of goods that sets the price, but the usefulness of the last unit one is prepared to acquire or give up: marginal utility. Water is so abundant that one more glass barely changes the life of the person who drinks it; the diamond is so rare that one more stone remains precious even to someone who already owns some. Smith's paradox vanishes as soon as we stop comparing masses and start comparing units.

## Two Schools Born of the Same Find

Yet the simultaneous discovery does not produce a single school. Jevons and Walras, by formalizing marginal utility through mathematics and equilibrium calculation (Walras responds in particular to a problem posed by the economist Antoine Augustin Cournot, that of the existence of a simultaneous equilibrium across all markets at once), found what becomes the dominant neoclassical economics. Menger, by contrast, refuses to reduce utility to a calculable number and insists on the judgment specific to each individual; his lineage, extended by Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk and then by Friedrich Hayek, becomes the Austrian school. Hayek will acknowledge, in 1934, that the founding ideas of this school belong entirely to Menger. A century and a half later, the two branches, born on the same day from the same problem, still disagree over what a price actually measures.

repere.texte: Jevons publishes his theory of marginal utility in 1871 in Manchester, Menger the same year in Vienna, Walras three years later in Lausanne: three economists, in three countries, with no knowledge of the other two's work.

carte.punch: Three economists, three countries, no contact: the same discovery between 1871 and 1874.
carte.idee: In 1871, Jevons in Manchester and Menger in Vienna, unaware of each other, publish the same solution to the water-diamond paradox posed by Adam Smith. Walras rediscovers it in Lausanne three years later. From this same find come two schools of economics that are still rivals today.

quiz.question: How do Jevons, Menger, and Walras resolve the water-diamond paradox posed by Adam Smith?
choix: By distinguishing the usefulness of the last available unit from the usefulness of the whole category
By demonstrating that water actually costs more to produce than diamonds
By proving that the price of a diamond reflects only its cost of extraction
By doing away with the notion of value in favor of market price alone
quiz.explication: The paradox vanishes once we compare, not the total usefulness of all water or all diamonds, but the usefulness of one more unit: an extra glass of water counts for little because water is so abundant, while one more diamond remains precious because diamonds are so rare. None of the three invokes production cost.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What problem does Léon Walras also seek to solve, in addition to the water-diamond paradox?
choix: Calculating the exact amount of English monetary devaluations
A simultaneous equilibrium across all markets, posed by Cournot
Determining the economy's natural rate of interest
The complete classification of goods into market categories
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Walras responds in particular to a problem posed by the economist Antoine Augustin Cournot, that of the existence of a simultaneous equilibrium across all markets at once.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Carl Menger differ from Jevons and Walras in their shared discovery?
choix: He takes no interest in the water-diamond paradox
He formalizes marginal utility through general equilibrium calculation
He refuses to reduce utility to a calculable number
He publishes his work twenty years after the other two
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Menger insists on the judgment specific to each individual rather than on mathematical calculation, unlike Jevons and Walras; his lineage, extended by Böhm-Bawerk and then Hayek, becomes the Austrian school.
